paragraphs: Regularization guides a neural network toward solutions with desirable behavior beyond fitting its training examples. This paper proposes understanding several regularization methods through a common mathematical quantity: the norm associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. That perspective gives different training penalties a shared reference point for describing and controlling the learned function.

The central practical obstacle is that this norm cannot be computed directly. The authors instead use upper and lower approximations that lead to usable training strategies. Through these approximations, they connect spectral norm penalties, gradient penalties, and adversarial training. They also derive new penalties and suggest combining upper and lower bounds to approximate the underlying norm more closely.

Experiments support the approach for learning from small datasets and for producing models resistant to adversarial perturbations. Its contribution therefore combines an organizing explanation of existing methods with additional regularization choices. The reported effectiveness concerns those experimental settings; the shared mathematical perspective does not make every approximation equally effective in every application.
icml-2019-a-kernel-perspective-for-regul.tldr: Approximations to an RKHS norm unify existing neural-network regularizers and motivate new penalties effective in small-data and adversarial-robustness experiments.

paragraphs: A function with many input parameters can be difficult to approximate or interpret. This paper introduces Active Manifolds, a nonlinear approach to simplifying the analysis of continuously differentiable functions. Under appropriate hypotheses, it identifies a one-dimensional curve in the input space along which nearly all of the function’s values are attained.

The curve provides a simpler setting for approximation and sensitivity analysis, even when the original input space has many dimensions. The authors supply theoretical justification and an algorithm for using it. Unlike a single summary of overall parameter influence, analysis along the curve can reveal how each parameter’s influence changes at different locations, with results displayed in two-dimensional plots.

On accessible low-dimensional examples, the method reduces approximation error by an order of magnitude relative to Active Subspaces, while requiring more computation. An application to a magnetohydrodynamic power-generator model also reveals parameter information that Active Subspaces misses. These results support a tradeoff: more computational work can yield more accurate approximation and richer sensitivity analysis in the examined settings.
icml-2019-active-manifolds-a-non-linear-.tldr: Active Manifolds uses a nonlinear curve to simplify function analysis, improving approximation and sensitivity information in examples at additional computational cost.

paragraphs: Node embeddings represent graph nodes using compact vectors that retain useful information about the network’s structure. Those vectors then support downstream prediction tasks. This paper investigates whether an adversary can undermine that process by changing the graph from which the representations are learned, focusing on the widely used family of methods based on random walks.

The authors derive efficient adversarial changes to the network structure. These changes poison the input to representation learning, so their effects can extend beyond the graph itself to both the learned vectors and the tasks that depend on them. The analysis therefore examines the reliability of a shared representation-building stage, rather than only the behavior of a particular downstream predictor.

The reported attacks damage embedding quality and downstream performance. They also transfer across many models and remain successful under restrictions on the attacker. This means the demonstrated vulnerability is not confined to one attacked model. The findings establish robustness concerns for the investigated methods, without implying that every graph representation method or every restricted attacker behaves identically.
icml-2019-adversarial-attacks-on-node-em.tldr: Efficient changes to graph structure can degrade random-walk-based node embeddings and downstream tasks, with attacks transferring across multiple models.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether adversarial vulnerability comes from insufficient information or from the computational difficulty of learning robust classifiers. It first proves that, for a broad class of tasks, the existence of a robust classifier implies that relatively few training examples suffice to find one. The catch is that the search algorithm may require exponential time.

The authors then construct two high-dimensional binary classification tasks that separate ordinary learning from robust learning. Both permit efficient ordinary classification with a simple linear separator. Both also admit robust learning with sufficiently powerful computation, even for large perturbations. Yet efficient robust learning is ruled out even for small perturbations within the respective hardness settings.

For one construction, the barrier applies to efficient algorithms in the statistical query model. For the other, it depends on a cryptographic assumption. These results establish exponential separations under those conditions. They support computational constraints as a possible explanation for adversarial examples, rather than proving that computation explains every observed vulnerability or that robustness is universally impossible.
icml-2019-adversarial-examples-from-comp.tldr: Constructed classification tasks show that robust learning can require far more computation than ordinary learning despite needing relatively little data.

paragraphs: Data collected for a useful purpose can also reveal sensitive attributes unrelated to that purpose. A facial image or an incidental recording, for example, may support more inferences than the person providing it intended. This paper addresses the tension between preserving useful individualized services and reducing the sensitive information carried by the data used for those services.

The authors formulate the problem using information theory and implement their approach as an unconstrained adversarial game between deep neural networks. The competing objectives guide the learning of stochastic transformations: procedures that introduce randomness when converting input data into another representation. The transformations preserve the data domain, allowing existing algorithms to continue operating on the transformed information.

The stated outcome is a way to maintain performance on existing algorithms while minimizing sensitive-information leakage. This makes compatibility with useful inference part of the privacy-oriented learning problem itself. The claim is about balancing utility and reduced leakage through learned transformations; minimizing leakage does not amount to a stated guarantee that all sensitive information disappears.
icml-2019-adversarially-learned-represen.tldr: An information-theoretic adversarial learning approach produces randomized data transformations that preserve useful inference while minimizing sensitive-information leakage.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants train on local data and send parameter updates to a server that combines them into a global model. This paper studies model poisoning: an attacker manipulates the updates contributed by a small number of participants, usually one, to make the global model confidently misclassify chosen inputs.

The authors begin with an attack that amplifies a malicious update so it can overcome other participants’ contributions. They then introduce two notions of stealth for identifying suspicious updates and incorporate those considerations into the attacker’s objective. An alternating optimization strategy improves stealth by switching between pursuing the targeted misclassification and making the update appear less suspicious.

The experiments also show that the Byzantine-resilient aggregation strategies examined do not withstand these attacks. Together, the findings indicate that even highly constrained attackers can influence a federated model while remaining stealthy under the considered criteria. Sharing updates instead of raw data therefore leaves an important integrity problem: a participant’s contribution can be malicious even when the underlying data stays local.
icml-2019-analyzing-federated-learning-t.tldr: A small number of malicious federated-learning participants can cause targeted errors through stealthy model updates, defeating the aggregation defenses examined.

paragraphs: This paper studies online classification into K classes when each example is a point in a d-dimensional space. The learner receives bandit feedback, making its learning problem more restricted than classification with full label information. The central question is whether efficient algorithms can make only finitely many mistakes when the classes are linearly separable with a positive margin.

The authors distinguish strong and weak forms of linear separability. Under the strong condition, they provide an efficient algorithm with a near-optimal mistake bound proportional to K divided by the square of the margin. This expresses how the guarantee depends on both the number of possible classes and the separation available between them.

Under weak separability, they also obtain an efficient algorithm with a finite mistake bound, but its dependence on the problem parameters is substantially larger and exponential. That method uses a kernel Perceptron approach. The results make progress on the broader challenge while preserving a crucial distinction: the stronger assumption supports a much tighter guarantee than the weaker one.
icml-2019-bandit-multiclass-linear-class.tldr: Efficient bandit classifiers achieve finite mistake bounds under two separability conditions, with a near-optimal bound under the stronger condition.

paragraphs: The paper addresses minimizing a smooth convex function over a polytope, a feasible region defined by flat boundaries. Its method blends Frank–Wolfe, also known as conditional gradient, with additional gradient-based steps. These added steps differ from away steps and pairwise steps, while the resulting algorithm retains linear convergence when the objective is strongly convex.

A practical attraction is that the algorithm avoids projecting points back onto the feasible region. It also represents each iterate as a sparse convex combination of a limited number of extreme points. Its lazy implementation uses inexpensive, inexact solutions to the linear programming subproblem that normally drives conditional gradient methods, reducing the need for costly exact work.

The authors report rapid reductions in both primal and dual gaps, which measure progress toward optimality, in iteration counts and elapsed time. Their comparisons outperform even the cited lazy conditional gradient methods. They also give a streamlined version for the probability simplex. The contribution combines these practical benefits with a convergence guarantee whose linear rate specifically requires strong convexity.
icml-2019-blended-conditonal-gradients-7.tldr: Blending conditional gradients with gradient-based steps preserves sparse, projection-free optimization and achieves linear convergence for strongly convex objectives.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into representations used by systems such as recommenders and models of social networks. The paper addresses fairness constraints on those representations, including requests that they not correlate with attributes such as age or gender. Its motivation is that useful graph representations should be able to accommodate such constraints alongside their predictive role.

The authors introduce an adversarial framework whose central feature is compositionality. Different fairness constraints can be combined during inference, allowing the requested combination to vary across uses of the same framework. In the recommendation example, one user could request invariance to both age and gender, while another could request invariance only to age.

Experiments on knowledge-graph and recommender-system benchmarks demonstrate the framework’s utility. The contribution is therefore more specific than applying one fixed fairness restriction during representation learning: it supports flexible combinations at inference time. The fairness objective here concerns the stated attribute-related constraints on representations and recommendations, which is the particular form of fairness the framework is designed to address.
icml-2019-compositional-fairness-constra.tldr: An adversarial graph-embedding framework allows different combinations of attribute-related fairness constraints to be requested at inference time.

paragraphs: Design problems often ask for an object with a desired property, such as a protein with greater fluorescence. This paper considers both maximizing properties and specifying their desired values. It assumes access to black-box stochastic predictors that map a candidate design to a distribution over the properties of interest, rather than supplying only a single predicted value.

Directly optimizing such predictors can be problematic because predictive models may behave poorly far from their training distribution. A search for attractive predictions can therefore encounter regions where the predictor itself is unreliable. This concern changes the design problem: the objective involves finding promising designs through imperfect predictive information, rather than simply seeking the largest oracle output.

The proposed method uses model-based adaptive sampling to estimate a distribution over designs conditioned on the desired properties. Its output is thus a distribution of candidates associated with the design goal. The approach frames design as learning where to sample given a target, with stochastic property predictions serving as the assumed source of information.
icml-2019-conditioning-by-adaptive-sampl.tldr: Adaptive sampling estimates a distribution of designs conditioned on desired properties using stochastic black-box predictors that may be unreliable away from training data.

paragraphs: Ordered k-Median is a clustering problem in which points receive weights according to their rank in distance from the chosen centers. Different weight choices express different clustering objectives, including classical k-Median and k-Center. This paper develops small summaries of a dataset that preserve these objectives well enough to accelerate clustering computations.

Such a summary, called a coreset, is a weighted collection of points whose objective value approximates that of the full data for every possible set of k centers. The authors strengthen this requirement: their simultaneous coreset works for every weight choice as well. That matters when users want to explore multiple clustering priorities without constructing a separate summary for each.

The main construction has size proportional to k squared times the squared logarithm of the dataset size, with additional dependence on dimension and approximation accuracy. Its guarantee preserves objective values within a factor of one plus or minus the chosen error tolerance. On a real geographical dataset, the authors report a large computational speedup while maintaining high accuracy across a range of weights.
icml-2019-coresets-for-ordered-weighted-.tldr: A simultaneous coreset compresses clustering data while approximating Ordered k-Median costs for every choice of centers and weights.

paragraphs: Traditional bandit problems seek the option with the highest average reward. This paper studies a different objective: choosing the option that best helps estimate all the others. Motivated by settings such as sensor placement and cellular-network monitoring, it defines quality through the mean-squared error of those estimates. Learning correlations is therefore central to choosing well.

The authors first construct an estimator of this error using sample variances and covariances. They prove exponential concentration around the true error, giving theoretical control over how misleading the estimate can be. This provides the statistical foundation for comparing options according to their information about the whole collection, rather than according to their individual means.

They then propose a successive-rejection-style algorithm for identifying the best option and bound its probability of selecting incorrectly. A minimax analysis also establishes fundamental performance limits for the problem. Together, these contributions formulate the alternative objective, provide an algorithm with guarantees, and characterize constraints on how well correlated-bandit identification can perform.
icml-2019-correlated-bandits-or-how-to-m.tldr: Correlated bandits select the option that best estimates all options, using covariance-based error estimates and an identification algorithm with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, solves imperfect-information games through repeated traversal of the game tree and converges to an equilibrium. For very large games, a common approach first compresses the game through abstraction, solves that smaller version using tables, and transfers the resulting strategy back to the original game.

The paper explains several problems with this workflow. Abstraction often requires manual, domain-specific decisions and can discard strategically important distinctions. Choosing a good abstraction also creates a circular difficulty: knowing what can safely be simplified may require knowledge of the equilibrium that the algorithm is supposed to discover. These issues motivate learning directly in the full game.

Deep CFR replaces the need for that preliminary abstraction with deep neural networks that approximate CFR’s behavior. The authors present it as a principled method and demonstrate strong performance in large poker games, describing it as the first successful non-tabular CFR variant at that scale. The result supports neural approximation as a practical route to applying CFR beyond explicit tabular representations.
icml-2019-deep-counterfactual-regret-min.tldr: Deep CFR uses neural networks to approximate CFR in full games, avoiding preliminary abstraction and achieving strong results in large poker games.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations becomes restrictive when the demonstrator performs poorly. The paper argues that conventional inverse reinforcement learning often seeks a reward function that makes the observed behavior appear nearly optimal. That objective can obscure the demonstrator’s underlying intention when the intention was executed badly, limiting how far a learner improves beyond the examples.

Trajectory-ranked Reward EXtrapolation, or T-REX, instead learns rewards from demonstrations with approximate rankings. The relative ordering supplies information about which observed behaviors are better, even if none is especially strong. The learned reward is intended to extrapolate beyond those demonstrations and can then guide deep reinforcement learning toward improved behavior.

On multiple Atari and MuJoCo tasks, T-REX combined with deep reinforcement learning outperforms the compared imitation-learning and inverse-reinforcement-learning methods. Performance is often more than twice that of the best demonstration. The authors also demonstrate robustness to noisy rankings and reward inference from observing a learner improve noisily over time. These findings support learning useful intentions from imperfectly executed, imperfectly ranked examples.
icml-2019-extrapolating-beyond-suboptima.tldr: T-REX learns rewards from approximately ranked demonstrations, enabling reinforcement-learning agents to substantially outperform imperfect demonstrators in tested tasks.

paragraphs: Using machine learning on sensitive data raises a practical tension between predictive accuracy, information security, and computational cost. Homomorphic encryption has been combined with neural networks to protect information during inference, but prior approaches restrict usable network width and depth and can be slow even for relatively simple networks. This paper presents two solutions to those constraints.

The first changes how data is represented during computation. The authors report more than a tenfold improvement in latency compared with prior attempts at the same security level, while also enabling wider networks. This links computational representation to both faster responses and the ability to use network architectures that previous approaches had difficulty supporting.

The second solution applies transfer learning to provide private inference with deep networks at approximately 0.16 seconds of latency. The authors demonstrate their methods on several computer-vision tasks. The two results address related deployment barriers through different approaches: one improves encrypted computation through data representation, while the other uses transfer learning to support fast private inference with deep models.
icml-2019-low-latency-privacy-preserving.tldr: New computational data representations and a transfer-learning approach substantially reduce latency for privacy-preserving neural-network inference in computer-vision demonstrations.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical data collected by other policies. This is challenging because the available observations reflect earlier decision-making behavior. The paper introduces a doubly robust estimator for reinforcement-learning evaluation, drawing on Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation, a principle developed in statistical causal inference.

The authors also develop several variance-reduction techniques to improve the estimator’s performance. Reducing variance addresses how much an evaluation estimate fluctuates with the available data. Their empirical comparisons span multiple reinforcement-learning environments and different degrees of model misspecification, allowing the evaluation to include settings where modeling choices do not accurately capture the underlying problem.

Across the tested conditions, the proposed estimator beats the existing methods considered. The paper also advances the theoretical analysis of off-policy estimators by establishing a convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of sample size, in probability, and characterizing their asymptotic distribution. These results combine favorable experimental comparisons with a description of estimation behavior as data increases.
icml-2019-more-efficient-off-policy-eval.tldr: A targeted-learning estimator with variance reduction improves off-policy evaluation across tested environments and comes with asymptotic statistical analysis.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization relies on sampled data, and variability in those samples can slow progress. Adaptive importance sampling aims to improve convergence by changing how samples are selected. This paper introduces a variance-reduction framework that combines several predefined sampling distributions, allowing existing knowledge about the data to be expressed through the available sampling choices.

The distributions themselves remain fixed, while their mixture weights change during optimization. This separates the design of candidate sampling patterns from learning how much emphasis each should receive. The proposed method, VRM, efficiently adapts those weights and can also work with distributions over sets of points, extending the framework beyond sampling choices that concern only individual points.

The theoretical result is asymptotic recovery of the best mixture weights in hindsight. That guarantee concerns the available predefined distributions and behavior in the limit, rather than immediate optimality at every training step. Experiments across a range of applications demonstrate the method’s versatility. The contribution is an adaptive way to combine sampling knowledge within the optimization process.
icml-2019-online-variance-reduction-with.tldr: VRM reduces stochastic-optimization variance by adapting weights over fixed sampling distributions and asymptotically recovering the best mixture in hindsight.

paragraphs: Mean field inference for discrete graphical models is generally highly nonconvex, including for probabilistic log-submodular models. Consequently, methods such as coordinate ascent typically reach local optima without establishing how good those solutions are globally. This paper develops mean field methods with strong approximation guarantees for the log-submodular setting and its posterior-agreement problem.

The main tool is DR-DoubleGreedy, an algorithm for continuous DR-submodular maximization subject to box constraints, which bound individual variables. It completes one pass with linear time complexity and achieves an optimal one-half approximation ratio. This provides a quantitative guarantee for the stated optimization class rather than requiring the algorithm to find an exact global optimum.

The authors apply this optimization technique to inference and compare their methods with baselines on synthetic and real-world datasets, reporting superior performance. The contribution thus connects a broadly useful optimization result with a specific family of probabilistic inference problems. Its guarantees rely on the stated problem structure; they do not extend automatically to arbitrary nonconvex mean field objectives.
icml-2019-optimal-continuous-dr-submodul.tldr: A linear-time double-greedy algorithm achieves an optimal one-half approximation for box-constrained continuous DR-submodular maximization and supports provable mean field inference.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks aim to learn dependencies across sequences, but truncated backpropagation through time cuts gradient propagation off at a fixed horizon. Real Time Recurrent Learning avoids this truncation and supports online training, yet its computational cost is impractically large. Approximations reduce that cost by introducing noise into the learning calculation.

This paper introduces Optimal Kronecker-Sum Approximation, or OK, as a new approximation to Real Time Recurrent Learning. The authors prove optimality within a specified class of approximations that includes all previously published approaches considered by the paper. That is a class-specific theoretical result, connecting the method to existing alternatives without claiming optimality over every conceivable training procedure.

The empirical results indicate negligible approximation noise in the examined settings. OK matches truncated backpropagation on character-level Penn TreeBank and exceeds it on a synthetic string-memorization task by exploiting online parameter updates. These findings show that avoiding truncation through approximation can remain competitive on a real-world task and offer benefits on a task where the online updates help.
icml-2019-optimal-kronecker-sum-approxim.tldr: OK provides a class-optimal approximation to untruncated recurrent-network learning, matching truncated backpropagation on one task and outperforming it on synthetic memorization.

paragraphs: Lossy compression traditionally balances the number of bits used against distortion in the reconstructed data. Yet a reconstruction with low numerical distortion need not have high perceptual quality, and improving one can worsen the other. This paper extends the analysis to treat rate, distortion, and perception as three distinct quantities that must be considered together.

The authors adopt an existing mathematical definition of perceptual quality and study the resulting three-way tradeoff. They show that requiring high perceptual quality generally raises the rate-distortion curve. In practical terms, imposing that additional requirement typically demands either more bits or greater distortion, even when a compression method is judged favorably by the traditional two-way analysis.

The paper proves fundamental properties of the tradeoff, derives a closed-form expression for a Bernoulli source, and provides a visual illustration using a toy MNIST example. These contributions explain why perceptually appealing compression can carry a measurable cost elsewhere. The result is a framework for reasoning about competing objectives, rather than assuming that improving a distortion measure also improves perceived quality.
icml-2019-rethinking-lossy-compression-t.tldr: Adding perceptual quality to compression theory reveals a three-way tradeoff in which better perception generally requires sacrificing bit rate or distortion.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient training commonly presents examples in random order. Although this spreads examples through an epoch, smaller portions may fail to preserve informative structure found in the full dataset. This paper investigates whether carefully arranging examples can make training more effective by ensuring that partial passes retain useful relationships present in the complete data.

The authors study this idea for matrix factorization, where embeddings of entities such as queries, videos, or words are learned from pairwise associations. They construct self-similar arrangements that preserve weighted Jaccard similarities among rows and columns. Their hypothesis is that such structure can let a single epoch deliver some of the benefits normally associated with multiple passes.

Experiments on synthetic and recommendation datasets show training acceleration ranging from 3% to 37%. The results support example arrangement as a potentially useful addition to stochastic gradient training in the studied setting. They leave the broader proposition appropriately exploratory: the paper demonstrates gains for matrix factorization and presents principled ordering as a direction deserving further investigation.
icml-2019-self-similar-epochs-value-in-a.tldr: Structure-preserving arrangements of training examples accelerate matrix-factorization training by 3%–37% in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper uses contextual bandits to select price incentives that guide electricity demand toward a target. At each round, a desired mean consumption is specified. Actual mean consumption is modeled as a complex function of the distribution of offered prices and contextual information, including temperature and weather, so effective price selection must account for changing conditions.

The proposed strategies adapt ideas from established contextual-bandit methods such as LinUCB. Performance is measured through quadratic losses, which penalize deviations from the target, and analyzed using regret. The authors establish regret upper bounds growing as T to the two-thirds power, apart from polylogarithmic factors, and obtain faster rates when stronger assumptions hold.

Simulations use a real UK Power Networks dataset involving price incentives. The results indicate that the strategies can choose useful price levels and may support demand-response management. The evidence therefore combines theoretical tracking guarantees with data-based simulation results; the stated practical finding is promising demand control through price selection, rather than a demonstrated guarantee of exact target attainment.
icml-2019-target-tracking-for-contextual.tldr: Contextual-bandit strategies choose electricity-price incentives to track consumption targets, with regret bounds and encouraging simulations on real demand-response data.

paragraphs: Word embeddings can encode stereotypes, including gender bias, that may be amplified when downstream machine-learning systems use them. Although methods exist to mitigate such biases, this paper focuses on understanding how they arise during training. It asks which parts of the training corpus contribute to the bias observed in an already learned embedding.

The authors develop a technique that reveals how changes to the training corpus would affect the resulting embedding bias. This connects a property of the learned representation back to particular source documents. That connection can identify document subsets whose removal would most reduce bias, making the analysis relevant to decisions about the training data itself.

The methodology is demonstrated on Wikipedia and New York Times corpora, where the authors report high accuracy. Its main contribution is therefore a way to trace and assess the origins of embedding bias, complementing efforts that modify representations after training. The stated findings support accurate attribution in the examined corpora, rather than claiming that document removal eliminates every form of stereotypical behavior.
icml-2019-understanding-the-origins-of-b.tldr: A corpus-perturbation analysis traces word-embedding bias to training documents and identifies document subsets whose removal would most reduce it.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes reproducing a computational procedure from reproducing the scientific conclusion drawn from it. A method may reliably generate the same numerical result, while the broader finding fails when relevant aspects of the experiment vary. The title highlights this difference: reproducible methods can still support conclusions that do not hold up across experiments.

The authors provide deep-learning experiments in which results can be reproduced, yet a slightly different experiment no longer supports the original finding. They argue that evaluation should account for essential sources of variation, rather than treating deterministic reruns as sufficient evidence. The concern is whether the empirical conclusion survives meaningful changes, not simply whether the original computation can be repeated.

The paper advocates more rigorous and varied empirical methodologies while recognizing the value of making methods easy to reproduce. It also seeks to clarify the distinction between exploratory work and empirical research. Its position is explicitly pluralistic: it promotes stronger support for conclusions without prescribing one new methodology or criticizing the role of exploration in deep-learning research.
icml-2019-unreproducible-research-is-rep.tldr: Repeatable numerical results can support fragile conclusions, so reproducibility also requires testing empirical findings across essential sources of variation.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks sometimes generalize better despite having more parameters. This paper investigates a possible explanation in a specific convolutional-network setting. The proposed mechanism combines feature exploration at initialization with weight clustering, linking what the network can initially represent to how training organizes its weights and which solutions gradient descent ultimately reaches.

The theoretical analysis uses a three-layer convolutional network with max-pooling on a newly defined extension of the XOR problem. In that setting, the interaction between exploration and clustering causes overparameterized networks to converge to global minima with better generalization than the global minima reached by smaller networks. Thus, reaching a global minimum alone does not settle the comparison.

Experiments with a three-layer convolutional network on MNIST also demonstrate the phenomena discussed in the analysis. The contribution is a concrete theoretical and empirical account of how extra parameters can help in certain cases. Its scope remains tied to the analyzed architecture and setting, rather than establishing that increasing any model’s size must improve its generalization.
icml-2019-why-do-larger-models-generaliz.tldr: In a specific convolutional-network setting, extra parameters improve generalization through the interaction of initial feature exploration and weight clustering.
